longread.title: Decathlon caps, ice cubes, and the soft side of male friendship
longread.snippet: Nikolai Voelcker stages hyper-detailed scenes of young men hanging out, finding surreal tenderness in everyday sportswear and messy living rooms.
body: Before he ever picked up a camera to explore the quiet dynamics of male companionship, Nikolai Voelcker was a boy in Zurich's Kreis 2 district who memorised the weekly programming grids of German-language television channels. That early love for broadcasting turned into a formal apprenticeship and diploma at Switzerland's national public broadcaster, SRF. He spent several years bouncing through its departments, hooked on the mechanics of entertainment, news shows, and visual pacing.

A spontaneous itch to live abroad led him first to UCLA for a summer of film production—an era he remembers feeling straight out of an American teen movie, complete with red cups, frat parties, and making out in half-broken cars perched on the Hollywood hills overlooking Los Angeles. After returning home to work as a video editor and animator, a three-month attempt to settle in Paris fell flat against a language barrier. London ultimately became his home, where he has spent the past three years directing, filming, and photographing.

His visual work carries the distinct grammar of his television background. His frames are meticulously constructed, balancing theatrical staging with intimate realism. Voelcker gathers young men into domestic spaces—draped over furniture, leaning against one another, their faces locked in deadpan seriousness. He uses this deliberate artifice to spotlight something rarely depicted with nuance: the physical closeness, affection, and quiet tenderness that exist between male friends.

The clothing and props ground each photograph firmly in modern British youth culture. In his shot titled A Hanging Harry, staged inside a house that once belonged to a close friend, the friction between mundane humor and precise composition is striking. The image captures a Decathlon cap, a phone tucked casually into Ralph Lauren underwear, and a remarkably deadpan expression on a boy busy annoying his friend. The models were non-professionals, navigating a shoot where the weather flipped from bright sunshine to rain every ten minutes.

Voelcker admits to being a planner by nature, confessing that he tends to overprepare so he does not lose his footing on set. He spends extensive time talking with his subjects beforehand, breaking down the concept so that everyone feels safe, comfortable, and confident. For him, the human experience of the set matters just as much as the frame; the ultimate goal is ensuring everyone involved is having a genuinely good day.

Yet some of his most striking frames emerge when strict planning collapses into chance. In a photograph from his Sydenham series, a group of young men were captured completely absorbed in an impromptu activity involving ice cubes. Set against a mix of accessories like a Gucci cap and an England football shirt, the spontaneous moment offered an oddly hypnotic focus and physical proximity that had never been scripted in his notes.

The power of the images lies right in that balance between high-concept compositing and real emotional resonance. The poses might be surreal, but the bonds feel authentic, hinting at inside jokes and shared history that linger long after the camera is packed away.

Looking forward, Voelcker is juggling upcoming exhibitions, project launches, an intimidating mountain of digital editing, and shipping out a batch of GTA 6 T-shirts. Perhaps most rewarding of all is the direct response from viewers: young men who see his portraits and recognise their own friendships, feeling seen in all their weird, affectionate reality.

items.title: The 2.6-ton stainless steel astronaut stuck in a Spanish roundabout
items.snippet: Just south of Madrid, drivers on their daily commute circle around a giant astronaut mid-stride on the surface of the Moon.
body: In the commuter town of Valdemoro, just south of Madrid, a giant visitor from another world looms over passing traffic. Standing four meters tall atop a dark mineral hemisphere meant to resemble the lunar surface, 'El Astronauta' captures a space explorer caught halfway through a monumental leap across the Moon—or perhaps simply trying to cross a suburban road.

Created by artist Francisco Leiro and installed in 2001, the statue stands at the center of a traffic circle suitably rechristened the Glorieta del Universo. The gleaming figure was designed to represent human progress and the desire to push past earthly limits, but over the last two decades, it has settled into something far more local: a beloved, surreal neighborhood icon.
more: Despite its lighthearted appearance, the sculpture is an immense engineering feat. It weighs roughly 2,600 kilograms and was fabricated out of heavy stainless steel at Fundición Capa in nearby Arganda del Rey. Producing the massive figure required casting it in approximately ten individual segments before welders assembled and polished the complete form.
The roundabout itself, originally known as the Rotonda de los Tritones, was specially finished with dark mineral material to mimic a fragment of moon rock under the astronaut's boots.

While Valdemoro is far better known for its proximity to neighboring Pinto than for any ties to space travel, the statue has turned the roundabout into one of the town's most recognized modern landmarks.
Today, the metallic figure stands alone on its miniature celestial body, giving passing motorists something vast to ponder during ordinary everyday traffic.

items.title: The Vietnamese citadel where two rival empires were built on top of each other
items.snippet: In the quiet countryside of An Nhon, medieval stone elephants and royal imperial tombs sit intertwined within the same overgrown walls.
body: Overlooking the fields of An Nhon, Vietnam, the Hoang De Citadel is a rare historical palimpsest where multiple rival dynasties physically stacked their empires upon the exact same plot of land.

It started in the eleventh century as Vijaya, the heavily fortified capital of the Champa Kingdom. Centuries later, in 1776, Emperor Nguyen Nhac took over the site and turned it into the central stronghold of the Tay Son movement. Today, the fortress gates conceal an eerie fusion of ancient spiritual relics and military fortifications.
more: Walking inside the citadel reveals layers of history pressed together in ways that feel almost accidental. Beneath overgrown earthen ramparts, visitors can spot eleventh-century Cham stone elephants and guardian carvings sitting side by side with the ruined foundations of eighteenth-century Tay Son palaces.

The site did not stop evolving after the Tay Son era, either. Following their fall, tombs and structures from the subsequent Nguyen Dynasty were erected within the same footprint, adding another chapter to the landscape.

The resulting site offers an unusual glimpse into shifting power in medieval and early modern Vietnam, presenting an atmospheric crossroads where warring cultures and their sacred art ended up sharing the same soil.

items.title: Why You Genuinely Don't Remember Having Your Own Embarrassing Opinions
items.snippet: Getting hit with a decade-old screenshot of your own bad take feels like an ambush, but science says your brain genuinely erased the evidence.
body: There are few modern experiences quite as humbling as delivering a righteous lecture online, only for someone to reply with a screenshot of you vehemently arguing the exact opposite position in 2013.

It turns out people caught in these 'is that you?' ambushes aren't always being deliberately dishonest. Human memory naturally rewrites its own history. Back in 1973, psychologists George Goethals and Richard Reckman measured students' views on school busing before having them debate the opposing side. After changing their minds, students misremembered their original beliefs as having always aligned with their new stance.
Your brain deletes the old draft to make you feel consistent. The only issue is that web archives and screenshots exist in high resolution.
more: Psychologists have spent decades documenting how we give ourselves grace that we rarely offer strangers. In 1997, Daniel Batson gave participants tasks to assign—one pleasant, one boring—recommending a coin flip to keep things fair. Around 90% of those who flipped the coin still awarded themselves the pleasant job regardless of the result. Batson dubbed this moral hypocrisy: the drive to appear principled without paying the cost.

Spotting hypocrisy in others is easy, but spotting it in ourselves is another story. In 2002, Emily Pronin identified the 'bias blind spot,' showing that people routinely rate themselves as less biased than everyone else. Our current opinions feel like objective common sense, while everyone else's look like opportunistic posturing.

Public figures have struggled with this record for decades. In 2004, John Kerry tried to defend an Iraq war vote by explaining he actually voted for the funding before voting against it, spawning a career-defining 'flip-flopper' attack ad. In 2012, Mitt Romney's campaign adviser described resetting their platform like shaking an Etch A Sketch—which opponents quickly weaponized as physical campaign props.

Unfortunately, the modern web has made shaking the Etch A Sketch impossible. The Wayback Machine has preserved over 800 billion pages, and deleting an old post usually just makes internet detectives dig deeper. The digital archive remembers everything with complete indifference to how much you've evolved.

items.title: Everyday Loopholes That Feel Illegal but Are Technically Allowed
items.snippet: From shifting hotel cancellation dates to walking confidently into luxury bathrooms, here are the cleverest technicalities of everyday life.
body: There is a peculiar thrill in finding a rule you can follow to the letter while completely violating its spirit. A recent viral thread asked people for life hacks that feel outright criminal but are completely above board.

The tricks range from pure audacity—like walking with brisk confidence into a luxury hotel lobby just to use a spotless restroom—to bureaucratic jujitsu. One standout: if you need to cancel a hotel reservation past the refund window, simply change your stay to a later date first, then cancel it once you're outside the penalty fee.
Researchers from MIT and Harvard note that these deliberate technicalities are common in human culture, exploiting the natural gap between what instructions say and what they actually intended.
more: A big category of modern loopholes revolves around exploiting corporate courtesy programs. Savvy travelers stagger their birth dates across different restaurant loyalty apps so free meals arrive once a month rather than in an unusable wave during a single week.

Others leverage corporate automation against itself. Drivers report nudging into traffic ahead of autonomous vehicles because sensor programs are hardcoded to brake and yield. Meanwhile, office workers admit that blaming arbitrary Microsoft updates or erratic Outlook email syncs works as an infallible, universally accepted excuse for being late on a deliverable.

Then there is personal social theater. One contributor admitted to emailing vendors as their own 'executive assistant' to confirm dinner reservations, instantly unlocking VIP treatment without spending an extra dime. Another has maintained that every vacation is their 'honeymoon' for a decade, scoring complimentary champagne and flight perks simply by holding hands.

Sociologists note that people readily embrace these workarounds because of a perceived power imbalance: outsmarting a large corporation feels like a harmless victory. As long as you aren't committing outright fraud, knowing how the machine operates is half the game.

items.title: Taking Screenshots Might Actually Be Stealing Your Memories
items.snippet: Your camera roll may be full of saved recipes and hilarious memes, but the very act of capturing them tricks your brain into forgetting.
body: Almost everyone treats their phone's screenshot gallery like a visual junk drawer. Between shopping lists, payment confirmations, and unhinged marketplace conversations, it's the fastest way to bookmark reality.

Surveys reveal that 97% of people use screenshots as a primary communication tool, forwarding visual evidence rather than typing out an explanation. In fact, research shows less than 40% of screenshots come from social media; the rest are practical breadcrumbs like maps, recipes, and learning materials.
However, outsourcing our memory to our photo roll comes with a strange cognitive side effect: taking the screenshot makes you significantly worse at actually remembering the thing you saved.
more: A 2025 study titled 'The Cost of Saving: How Photos and Screenshots Impair Memory' tracked participants looking at pieces of art. Some simply viewed the exhibits, while others preserved them using camera photos or screenshots.

The results across three experiments were clear: individuals who saved the images remembered the details far less accurately than those who merely looked at them. Grabbing a screenshot had a particularly sharp negative effect on recall.

When your phone makes it effortless to store an image, your brain assumes the information is secured in external storage and drops it from working memory. It's the digital counterpart to writing a note and never reading it again.

Despite the cognitive tax, users still invent practical workarounds with the tool. Some take screenshots of old photos simply to force them to the top of their gallery as temporary bookmarks, relying on image order to organize their day rather than digging through folders.

items.title: A free visual browser for After Effects' 600+ built-in presets
items.snippet: Jake In Motion releases Preset Browser, a free panel that finally lets you preview and organize AE's massive library of stock presets.
body: After Effects ships with more than 600 built-in animation and effect presets, but finding the right one has always been an exercise in frustration: you either memorize cryptic names or apply them blind to an empty layer.
Motion designer Jake Bartlett has launched Preset Browser, a completely free After Effects extension that adds a visual, searchable interface for every native preset included with the software.

In addition to displaying built-in options, the tool allows artists to generate video previews for their own custom user presets, turning chaotic personal preset folders into clean, visual asset libraries.
more: For decades, the Effects & Presets panel inside After Effects has remained essentially an unadorned list of folders. Knowing what an obscure text preset or background animation actually does meant digging through Adobe Bridge or repeatedly dropping presets onto dummy solids.
Preset Browser replaces that archaic workflow with a modern dockable panel. Users can hover and review animated previews of all 600+ default factory presets before committing them to the timeline.

Beyond browsing the native library, the extension functions as a custom asset manager. Motion designers can create custom collections, favorite go-to tools, and generate video preview clips for their own proprietary studio presets.
The tool includes categorized navigation, dynamic search, and customizable interface sizing so it can sit quietly alongside your active project workspace.

By making both factory tools and custom studio setups instantly previewable, Preset Browser fills a quality-of-life hole in the native After Effects software that animators have complained about for years.

items.title: Jake In Motion launches Design Mode for After Effects
items.snippet: A new extension brings dedicated vector editing directly into After Effects, ending the endless round-tripping to Illustrator.
body: Motion designer and educator Jake Bartlett (Jake In Motion) has released Design Mode, a dedicated vector editing suite running directly inside After Effects.

The tool is designed to solve one of the oldest pain points in motion design: hopping back and forth between Illustrator and After Effects just to make structural design tweaks. With Design Mode, artists can pull existing shape layers, masks, and text onto an editing canvas, refine them with actual design tools, and push the results directly back into the comp.

Crucially for animators, the extension respects keyframed properties. When you adjust paths or parameters that already have keyframes, Design Mode generates new keys to match the edits instead of breaking the timeline.
more: Round-tripping between Adobe Illustrator and After Effects has long been an accepted inefficiency in 2D animation pipelines. Minor shape tweaks or layout adjustments often require either re-importing artwork, converting vectors to shapes, or dealing with After Effects' notorious, clunky native pen and path manipulation tools.

Design Mode attacks this friction directly by creating an in-app vector workspace. You simply select your elements, bring them into the plugin's dedicated canvas, and use vector editing tools built specifically for designers.

Once adjustments are finished, pushing them back to the active composition updates the native shape layers, masks, and text layers cleanly. It avoids the mess of manually rebuilding layer structures or losing rig connections.

The keyframe integration is particularly valuable for existing animations. Editing properties that change over time doesn't flatten the layer; Design Mode adds appropriate keyframes at the current time, making iterative animation polish far more forgiving.

Design Mode is compatible with After Effects 2023 and newer on both Windows and macOS platforms, targeting commercial motion designers who want to iterate without constantly bouncing between separate desktop applications.
